en.title: Pharmacy: the whole course
en.short: What pharmacy is, how the degree is organised, the main areas and how to study it well.

sections.heading: Read this first
sections.text: These summaries teach concepts to students. They are not medical advice and do not replace teachers, textbooks, official guidance or the pharmacist’s professional judgement. They do not give drug doses. Clinical guidelines change and differ between countries, so check the current national guidance or World Health Organization (WHO) source. Anyone who is unwell should seek local medical help.

sections.heading: What pharmacy is
sections.text: Pharmacy is the health profession concerned with medicines: their discovery, preparation, quality, supply, safe use and the advice given to patients and prescribers. It combines chemistry, biology and pharmacology with law, ethics, communication and management. A pharmacist may work in a community pharmacy, hospital, industry, regulatory body, university or public health service. The work ranges from dispensing and compounding to medicine safety, research and policy.

sections.heading: How the degree is organised
sections.text: Pharmacy is studied as a university degree, but the length, award and registration route differ by country and institution. In Nigeria, programmes lead to a Bachelor of Pharmacy (BPharm) or Doctor of Pharmacy (PharmD), depending on the institution and current policy; they include supervised practical training and registration with the Pharmacists Council of Nigeria. In the United Kingdom, the MPharm is normally four years, followed by a foundation training year and registration with the General Pharmaceutical Council in Great Britain; Northern Ireland has its own regulator. Other countries have their own awards and internship rules. Check your own handbook and national regulator, because rules change.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The first topic, pharmacy as a profession, introduces roles, settings and professional identity. Teaching then usually begins with the scientific foundations: pharmaceutical calculations and measurement; general and organic chemistry; analytical chemistry; human anatomy and physiology; biochemistry and metabolism; microbiology and immunology. These explain the language, molecules, body and microbes that pharmacy depends on.

The pharmaceutical sciences follow: pharmaceutics and dosage forms; pharmacognosy and natural products; pharmacology; medicinal chemistry and drug design; biopharmaceutics and pharmacokinetics; formulation and manufacturing; pharmaceutical analysis and quality control; pharmaceutical microbiology and sterility assurance; compounding and dispensing.

Practice and patient care come next: pharmacy law, ethics and regulation; clinical pharmacy and patient care; pharmacotherapy of infectious diseases; pharmacotherapy of non-communicable diseases; pharmacovigilance and drug safety; community and hospital pharmacy practice; drug supply management and public health pharmacy; research methods and biostatistics.

At master’s level, students may study advanced pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics; pharmaceutical biotechnology and nanomedicine; advanced clinical pharmacy and pharmaceutical care; and a research dissertation.

sections.heading: How to study pharmacy
sections.text: Learn mechanisms before lists. Link each medicine to its target, its journey through the body and the patient problem it solves. Use calculations regularly, and check units and significant figures. Practise dispensing and compounding under supervision, and keep a notebook of errors. Test yourself with spaced questions, including calculations and case-based questions. Read product information and current national formularies, and learn to use reference sources rather than memorise every fact. Study in short, regular sessions and revise previous topics. Work in small groups to explain mechanisms aloud. Keep your ethics and communication skills alongside scientific knowledge, because pharmacy is a public trust.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text: Students often memorise drug lists without mechanisms, so they cannot reason about a new medicine or a patient with several conditions. Some treat calculations as a minor topic and then make unit errors. Others ignore quality control and sterility, although these protect patients. In law and ethics, students may quote one country’s rule as universal; always name the country and check the current regulator. In clinical work, a common error is to focus on the medicine and forget the patient’s kidney function, age, pregnancy, interactions and adherence. Another is to use these notes for self-treatment or to advise relatives. Do not do that; care needs a qualified pharmacist or clinician who can assess the person.

keyPoints: Pharmacy is the health profession that deals with medicines, from discovery and quality to supply and safe use.
Pharmacy degrees differ by country, so check your institution and national regulator for the award, length and registration route.
The course moves from scientific foundations to pharmaceutical sciences, practice, clinical care and research.
Learn mechanisms and calculations, not only lists, and test yourself regularly.
Guidelines and laws change and differ between countries, so use current official sources.
These summaries teach concepts and are not medical advice or a substitute for professional care.

en.title: Pharmacy as a profession: roles, settings and professional identity
en.short: The scope of pharmacy, its practice settings, teams, organisations, ethics and lifelong learning.

sections.heading: History and scope
sections.text:
Pharmacy is the health profession concerned with medicines: how they are discovered, developed, made, tested, supplied, dispensed and used safely. Its roots lie in preparing and selling remedies, but the modern profession grew as prescribing, dispensing and manufacturing separated and training and regulation became formal. Its scope runs from laboratory to bedside and shop counter.

A useful way to see the scope is the medicine lifecycle: research and development, formulation and production, quality assurance, distribution, dispensing and patient care, plus regulation and education. Each stage needs pharmaceutical knowledge, and each carries legal and ethical duties.

sections.heading: Practice settings
sections.text:
Community pharmacists work in public pharmacies. They dispense prescriptions, advise on safe use, and may offer screening or vaccination where national rules allow. Hospital pharmacists work in wards, dispensaries and sterile units, helping to manage medicines for inpatients and outpatients. Industrial pharmacists work in research, manufacturing, quality control, regulatory affairs and drug safety. Regulatory pharmacists work for agencies that approve, inspect and monitor medicines; examples include NAFDAC in Nigeria, the MHRA in the UK and the FDA in the United States. Academic pharmacists teach and research. Tasks and legal powers differ by country, so check local law and employer policy.

A short case: a student visits a community pharmacy in Ibadan. A woman brings a prescription and asks when to take her medicines. The pharmacist checks it, explains clearly, and refers her to the prescriber when a concern arises. The pharmacist is accessible, but also accountable.

sections.heading: Identity and learning
sections.text: Pharmacists work in interprofessional teams with doctors, nurses, laboratory staff and supply managers. Clear communication prevents error. Professional organisations support standards, advocacy and networking; the International Pharmaceutical Federation (FIP) is global, while national associations and regulators vary. Ethics means putting patient welfare first, keeping confidentiality, staying competent and being honest about errors. Lifelong learning, often called continuing professional development (CPD), keeps knowledge current; some countries require it to renew registration. Check your national regulator for rules that apply.

keyPoints: Pharmacy is the health profession concerned with the safe and effective use of medicines across their lifecycle.
Community, hospital, industry, regulatory and academic settings each need different pharmaceutical roles.
Legal powers and services vary by country, so check national law and regulator guidance.
Pharmacists work in interprofessional teams and must communicate clearly to prevent error.
Professional organisations support standards and advocacy; FIP is a global example.
Ethics and continuing professional development are central to professional identity.

en.title: Pharmaceutical calculations and measurement
en.short: SI units, density, percentage strength, dilution, alligation, displacement and isotonicity calculations.

sections.heading: Units and measurement
sections.text: Measurement uses SI base units: metre, kilogram, second, ampere, kelvin, mole and candela. The litre is accepted for volume and the pascal is an SI derived unit for pressure. Prefixes scale by powers of ten: milli is one thousandth, micro one millionth, kilo one thousand. Dimensional analysis, or the factor-label method, treats units as algebra: multiply by conversion factors so unwanted units cancel. Example: 2.5 g × 1000 mg/g = 2500 mg. Keep units in every step. These calculations support compounding and dispensing, not clinical dosing advice.

sections.heading: Density and strength
sections.text: Density is mass per volume, d = m/V. Specific gravity is the density of a substance divided by the density of water at a stated temperature; it has no units. Percentage strength states concentration. Weight/volume means grams per 100 mL, weight/weight means grams per 100 g, and volume/volume means millilitres per 100 mL. Example: 10 g in 200 mL is (10/200) × 100 = 5% w/v. Always state the basis; 5% w/v is not the same as 5% w/w.

sections.heading: Dilution and alligation
sections.text: Dilution uses C1V1 = C2V2, with concentration and volume in matching units. Example: to make 500 mL of 10% v/v from 50% v/v, V1 = (10 × 500)/50 = 100 mL; add 400 mL diluent. Alligation is a diagram method for mixing two strengths to reach a target. Mix 20% and 5% to make 10%: parts of 20% = 10 − 5 = 5; parts of 5% = 20 − 10 = 10; ratio 1:2. Check the final volume and strength.

sections.heading: Displacement and isotonicity
sections.text: Displacement volume is the volume occupied by a powder when it dissolves or disperses. Vehicle needed = final volume − displacement volume. Isotonicity means the same osmotic pressure as body fluid. Calculations use the sodium chloride equivalent (E value), the mass of sodium chloride with the same osmotic effect as 1 g of substance, or freezing point depression. Follow current pharmacopoeial methods and national guidance; standards differ by country.

keyPoints: SI prefixes scale units by powers of ten, and dimensional analysis converts units by cancelling them.
Density is mass divided by volume (d = m/V); specific gravity is density relative to water and has no units.
Percentage strength must state its basis: % w/v is grams per 100 mL, % w/w is grams per 100 g, and % v/v is millilitres per 100 mL.
Dilution follows C1V1 = C2V2 when concentration and volume units match.
Alligation gives the ratio of two strengths needed to reach a target strength.
Vehicle needed = final volume − displacement volume; isotonicity calculations use sodium chloride equivalents or freezing point depression according to current pharmacopoeial methods.

en.title: General and organic chemistry for pharmacy
en.short: Atomic structure, bonding, acids, equilibrium, mechanisms, functional groups and stereochemistry for drug molecules.

sections.heading: Atoms and bonding
sections.text:
Atoms have a nucleus of protons and neutrons, with electrons in orbitals. Electron configuration, especially valence electrons, explains bonding. Ionic bonds transfer electrons; covalent bonds share them. Polarity arises when atoms differ in electronegativity, giving partial charges and hydrogen bonding. These affect drug solubility, target binding and membrane passage.

Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Carbon forms four bonds and can make chains and rings.

sections.heading: Acids and equilibrium
sections.text:
An acid donates a proton (H+); a base accepts one. The acid dissociation constant Ka measures acid strength, and pKa = −log10 Ka. A lower pKa means a stronger acid. Weak acid or base drugs ionise according to pH and pKa, affecting absorption. Chemical equilibrium is when forward and reverse reaction rates are equal. The equilibrium constant K gives the ratio of products to reactants at equilibrium. Le Chatelier’s principle predicts the shift when conditions change.

Worked example: for an acid with pKa 4.5 at pH 7.4, pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA]), so 7.4 = 4.5 + log ratio; ratio = 10^2.9 ≈ 794. Ionised fraction = 794/(794+1) ≈ 0.999, about 99.9%.

sections.heading: Functional groups and names
sections.text: Functional groups are groups of atoms that give a molecule its characteristic reactions. Examples are hydroxyl (alcohol), carboxyl (acid), amino (base), ester, amide, ketone and aromatic ring. Nomenclature is a naming system. IUPAC names follow rules: find the longest carbon chain, number to give attached groups the lowest position numbers, and name functional groups with suffixes or prefixes. Drug names often use these rules, though approved names may differ.

sections.heading: Mechanisms and stereochemistry
sections.text:
A reaction mechanism describes bond breaking and making step by step, including curved arrows for electron movement. Common steps are nucleophilic attack, loss of a leaving group, and proton transfer. Mechanisms explain reaction rates and products.

Stereochemistry is the three-dimensional arrangement of atoms. A chiral centre has four different groups and gives two enantiomers, non-superimposable mirror images. Enantiomers can differ in biological activity, so stereochemistry matters for drugs. Geometric isomers differ around a double bond or ring.

keyPoints: Valence electrons and electronegativity explain ionic, covalent, polar and hydrogen bonding.
pKa = −log10 Ka; a lower pKa means a stronger acid.
pH = pKa + log([A−]/[HA]) describes ionisation of a weak acid.
Equilibrium is reached when forward and reverse rates are equal; Le Chatelier’s principle predicts shifts.
Reaction mechanisms describe electron movement and bond changes in steps.
A chiral centre has four different groups and gives enantiomers that may differ in biological activity.

en.title: Analytical chemistry: principles and techniques
en.short: Titrimetry, UV-visible and IR spectroscopy, chromatography, calibration, accuracy, precision and QC.

sections.heading: Titrimetry
sections.text:
Titrimetry finds an analyte’s concentration by adding a standard solution of known concentration until the reaction is complete. The equivalence point is where the amounts react exactly in proportion; an indicator or instrument marks the end point. A primary standard is a pure, stable substance used to standardise solutions.

Example: 25.0 mL of hydrochloric acid needs 20.0 mL of 0.100 M sodium hydroxide. Moles NaOH = 0.100 × 0.0200 = 0.00200 mol. The reaction is 1:1, so HCl is also 0.00200 mol. Concentration = 0.00200 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0800 M.

sections.heading: Spectroscopy
sections.text:
UV-visible spectroscopy measures light absorbed by a solution, 200 to 800 nm. The Beer-Lambert law links absorbance A to concentration c: A = ε × c × l, where ε is molar absorptivity and l is path length in cm.

Example: A = 0.450, ε = 1.5 × 10⁴ L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹, l = 1 cm. Then c = 0.450 ÷ 15000 = 3.0 × 10⁻⁵ M.

Infrared spectroscopy uses wavenumbers (cm⁻¹) to identify functional groups.

sections.heading: Chromatography
sections.text: Chromatography separates components between a stationary phase and a moving mobile phase. Components spending more time in the mobile phase travel faster. Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) uses a coated plate; the retention factor Rf is the distance moved by the spot divided by that moved by the solvent front. Column methods such as HPLC and gas chromatography (GC) give retention times for identification and quantification.

sections.heading: Calibration and quality
sections.text:
Calibration compares instrument response with known standards. A calibration curve plots response against concentration; the blank sets zero and the slope gives sensitivity. Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is closeness of repeated results to each other. Results can be precise yet inaccurate when a systematic error is present.

Quality control runs known-value samples with each batch on control charts. Good practice needs written procedures, trained staff, recorded data and validation. Pharmacopoeias and national regulators set official methods; check the current edition for your country.

keyPoints: Titrimetry: moles = concentration × volume in litres, and reactants combine in the ratio of the equation.
Beer-Lambert law: A = ε × c × l, so c = A ÷ (ε × l).
Chromatography separates by movement between a stationary and a mobile phase; Rf and retention time identify components.
Accuracy is closeness to the true value; precision is agreement between repeats, and both are needed.
Calibrate with standards and a blank, and run quality control samples with every batch.
Official methods and limits come from pharmacopoeias and national regulators and change; check the current edition.

en.title: Human anatomy and physiology for pharmacy
en.short: Cells, tissues, organ systems and homeostasis, focused on drug action and patient counselling.

sections.heading: Cells and tissues
sections.text:
Anatomy is body structure; physiology is how it works. The cell is the basic unit. It has a membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus. The membrane is a lipid bilayer with proteins. Some proteins are receptors that receive signals; others are transporters that move substances. Many medicines act at receptors, enzymes or transporters, but those actions belong to pharmacology.

Tissues are groups of similar cells. The four main types are epithelial tissue, which covers surfaces; connective tissue, which supports; muscle tissue, which contracts; and nervous tissue, which carries electrical signals. Organs combine tissues, and organ systems combine organs.

sections.heading: Organ systems
sections.text:
An organ system is a set of organs working together. Examples are the skin barrier; the cardiovascular system, which pumps blood; the respiratory system, which exchanges gases; the gastrointestinal system, which digests and absorbs; the renal system, which filters blood; the nervous system, which senses and controls; and the endocrine system, which releases hormones.

For pharmacy, the skin, gut, liver, kidneys, lungs and heart matter because they affect how a medicine is absorbed, distributed, changed or removed. They also explain side effects and warning signs. For example, a medicine that slows gut movement can cause constipation. Knowing normal structure helps you ask useful questions.

sections.heading: Homeostasis and counselling
sections.text:
Homeostasis is the body’s ability to keep internal conditions stable around a set point. In negative feedback, sensors detect a change, a control centre compares it with the set point, and effectors respond. For example, when body temperature rises, the hypothalamus signals sweating and widening of skin blood vessels, so heat is lost. Fever is a raised set point, not a failure of homeostasis.

A case: Amina has chronic kidney disease and asks why her medicine is reviewed. The kidneys filter blood and clear many medicines. If kidney function falls, a medicine may build up. The pharmacist explains this and asks her to report reduced urine or swelling. Local guidelines direct any change; she should not adjust treatment herself.

keyPoints: Anatomy is structure and physiology is function, with the cell as the basic unit of the body.
The cell membrane is a lipid bilayer with receptor and transporter proteins where many medicines act.
The four main tissue types are epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous.
Organs form organ systems such as cardiovascular, respiratory, gastrointestinal, renal and nervous.
Homeostasis uses negative feedback with sensors, a control centre, a set point and effectors.
Kidney or liver function can change medicine handling, so review and counselling must follow current national or World Health Organization guidance.

en.title: Biochemistry and metabolism
en.short: Biomolecules, enzymes, energy metabolism, protein synthesis, pathways and clinical biochemistry basics.

sections.heading: Biomolecules and enzymes
sections.text:
Biomolecules are the molecules of life: carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids. Carbohydrates supply energy; lipids form membranes and store energy; proteins build structures and catalyse reactions; nucleic acids store and transmit genetic information. Monomers join by condensation and split by hydrolysis.

Enzymes are protein catalysts that speed reactions. The active site binds substrate. Activity depends on pH, temperature and substrate concentration. Michaelis constant Km is the substrate concentration at half the maximum rate Vmax. The Michaelis-Menten equation is v = Vmax × [S] ÷ (Km + [S]). If Vmax is 100 units and Km is 5 mmol/L, at [S] = 5 mmol/L, v = 100 × 5 ÷ (5 + 5) = 50 units. Inhibitors may be competitive or non-competitive.

sections.heading: Energy metabolism
sections.text:
Energy metabolism converts food energy into ATP, the energy currency. Glycolysis breaks glucose to pyruvate in the cytoplasm, giving net 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose. Pyruvate enters mitochondria and becomes acetyl-CoA. The Krebs cycle oxidises acetyl groups, producing NADH, FADH2 and GTP.

Oxidative phosphorylation uses the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis to make most ATP. Anaerobic glycolysis produces lactate when oxygen is limited. ATP yield varies with the shuttle, so learn a range, not a fixed number.

sections.heading: Protein synthesis and pathways
sections.text:
Protein synthesis has transcription and translation. DNA is transcribed to messenger RNA, which is translated by ribosomes using transfer RNA and the genetic code. Each codon specifies an amino acid, except the three stop codons.

Metabolic pathways are linked enzyme-catalysed reactions, often linear, branched or cyclic, regulated by feedback inhibition, enzyme amount and hormone signals. Catabolism breaks molecules down to release energy; anabolism builds molecules and uses energy.

sections.heading: Clinical biochemistry basics
sections.text:
Clinical biochemistry measures substances in blood, urine or other fluids. Examples include glucose, electrolytes, creatinine, liver enzymes and lipids.

Results are compared with reference intervals, which vary by laboratory, age, sex and method. Interpret a single result with history and examination. Screening and treatment thresholds differ by country and change, so check current national or WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Biomolecules are carbohydrates, lipids, proteins and nucleic acids; monomers join by condensation and split by hydrolysis.
Enzymes are protein catalysts; Km is the substrate concentration at half Vmax, and v = Vmax × [S] ÷ (Km + [S]).
Glycolysis gives net 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose; the Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation produce most ATP.
Protein synthesis is transcription of DNA to mRNA followed by translation by ribosomes using the genetic code.
Metabolic pathways are regulated by feedback inhibition, enzyme amount and hormone signals; catabolism releases energy and anabolism uses it.
Clinical biochemistry results are compared with reference intervals and interpreted with history; thresholds vary by country and change, so check current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Microbiology and immunology for pharmacy
en.short: Bacterial structure, growth, sterilisation, resistance, immunity and vaccine principles.

sections.heading: Bacterial structure and growth
sections.text: Bacteria are prokaryotes with no nucleus. Most have a cell wall made of peptidoglycan, a mesh of sugars linked by short peptides. Gram staining divides them into Gram-positive, with a thick wall, and Gram-negative, with a thin wall and an outer membrane. Some have capsules, flagella, pili or spores. They grow by binary fission; in a closed culture, growth has lag, log (exponential), stationary and death phases. Generation time is the time for one cell to divide. Escherichia coli can double about every 20 minutes under ideal laboratory conditions. After 3 hours (180 minutes), that is 9 doublings, so one cell gives 2 to the power 9 = 512 cells.

sections.heading: Sterilisation and disinfection
sections.text: Sterilisation destroys or removes all microorganisms, including bacterial spores. Disinfection reduces harmful microorganisms on inanimate objects but may not kill spores. Antisepsis is disinfection applied to skin or tissue. Sterilisation methods include moist heat in an autoclave, dry heat, filtration and radiation. Disinfectants include alcohols and chlorine-releasing agents. Their activity depends on concentration, contact time and organic matter, so follow the manufacturer’s instructions.

sections.heading: Antimicrobial resistance
sections.text: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) means microorganisms survive medicines that once killed them. Bacteria may be intrinsically resistant or acquire resistance by mutation or by horizontal gene transfer. Mechanisms include enzymes that destroy the drug, pumps that expel it, altered drug targets and reduced permeability. Unnecessary antibiotic use and poor infection control select for resistant strains. Taking an antibiotic for a viral cold gives no benefit and may select resistant bacteria.

sections.heading: Immunity and vaccines
sections.text: Innate immunity is fast and non-specific: skin and mucus barriers, phagocytes, inflammation and complement, a set of blood proteins that help destroy microbes. Adaptive immunity is slower and specific, with memory. B cells make antibodies; T cells help B cells or kill infected cells. A vaccine presents a safe antigen, such as an inactivated toxin or a subunit protein, so the immune system forms memory without disease. Adjuvants are substances that strengthen the response. Vaccination protects others through herd immunity. Schedules differ by country; check current national guidance.

keyPoints: Bacteria are prokaryotes; Gram staining reflects differences in the cell wall.
Growth by binary fission is exponential: after n doublings, number = starting number × 2^n.
Sterilisation kills or removes all microorganisms including spores; disinfection may not.
Antimicrobial resistance can arise by mutation or horizontal gene transfer and is selected by unnecessary antibiotic use.
Innate immunity is fast and non-specific; adaptive immunity is specific and has memory.
Vaccines safely create immune memory; schedules differ by country, so check current national guidance.

en.title: Pharmaceutics: dosage forms and drug delivery
en.short: How medicines become solids, liquids, semisolids, parenterals, inhaled and topical forms for delivery.

sections.heading: Dosage forms
sections.text:
A dosage form is the physical form of a medicine. Solid forms include tablets, capsules and powders. Liquid forms include solutions, suspensions and emulsions; suspensions must be shaken. Semisolid forms include creams, ointments and gels.

Parenteral forms are sterile preparations given by injection. Inhaled forms deliver medicine to the lungs as aerosols or dry powders. Topical forms are applied to skin, eyes, ears or nose. The form affects release speed and site of action.

sections.heading: Excipients and routes
sections.text:
Excipients are inactive ingredients added to make a dosage form. They include fillers, binders, disintegrants, lubricants, preservatives, antioxidants, sweeteners, colours and coatings. They aid manufacture, stability, taste and release, but must be compatible with the active ingredient and safe for the patient.

A route of administration is the path by which medicine enters the body: oral, topical, parenteral, inhaled, rectal, vaginal or nasal. The route depends on the patient, the site of action and the medicine’s properties. A medicine destroyed in the stomach may need a parenteral or inhaled route.

sections.heading: Formulation and packaging
sections.text:
Formulation aims to deliver the right amount of active ingredient safely and reliably. The formulator considers solubility, stability, particle size, pH, taste and release profile. A product may be immediate-release or modified-release. Patient factors matter: age, ability to swallow and preferences.

Packaging protects from light, moisture, oxygen and contamination. It carries the label with name, strength, directions, batch number and expiry date. Some products need child-resistant or tamper-evident packaging. Case: a pharmacist in Ibadan has a patient who cannot swallow tablets. The medicine is stable in water but bitter. The pharmacist chooses an oral solution with a sweetener and preservative, checks compatibility and labels it clearly. National quality standards differ, so check the current official source.

keyPoints: A dosage form is the physical form of a medicine and it affects release and route.
Solid, liquid, semisolid, parenteral, inhaled and topical forms suit different medicines and patients.
Excipients are inactive ingredients that aid manufacture, stability, taste or release and must be compatible with the active ingredient.
The route of administration is the path into the body and depends on the patient, site of action and medicine properties.
Formulation balances solubility, stability, release profile and patient factors.
Packaging protects the product and carries the label; check current national quality standards.

en.title: Pharmacognosy and natural products
en.short: Medicinal plants, crude drugs, active constituents, standardisation, herbal quality, safety and traditional medicine.

sections.heading: Plants as medicines
sections.text:
Pharmacognosy is the study of medicines from natural sources, especially plants. A medicinal plant is a plant used to prevent or treat illness. Its effect usually comes from secondary metabolites, chemicals the plant makes that are not needed for basic growth. Major groups include alkaloids, glycosides, terpenoids and phenolics.

People use plant parts: leaf, bark, root, seed or flower. The same species can differ by part, season and place. That is why identity and source matter before any health claim is considered.

sections.heading: Crude drugs and constituents
sections.text:
A crude drug is natural material used as medicine with little processing, such as dried bark or leaf. It may come from plants, animals or minerals. Active constituents are the compounds mainly responsible for the effect. Examples include morphine from opium poppy, quinine from Cinchona bark and artemisinin from Artemisia annua.

Crude drugs are described by name, source, part and appearance. A phytochemical is a plant chemical studied for activity. Not every constituent is known, so a marker compound may be measured instead.

sections.heading: Standardisation and quality
sections.text:
Standardisation means making each batch consistent and within set limits. It checks identity, purity, strength and contamination. Tests may include macroscopic and microscopic examination, chromatography and chemical assays. A marker is a chosen compound used to compare batches, not always the only active one.

Quality problems include wrong species, wrong plant part, adulteration, heavy metals, pesticides, microbes and aflatoxins. Herbal products vary with soil, harvest and drying. Good manufacturing practice and a pharmacopoeia monograph help control this.

sections.heading: Safety and tradition
sections.text:
Herbal medicine is not automatically safe because it is natural. Risks include liver injury, allergic reactions, interactions with medicines and contamination. Pregnant women, children and people with long-term illness need care. This is education, not advice to use a plant.

Traditional medicine is knowledge and practice based on local beliefs and experience, often using plants. WHO supports safe, integrated use and national regulation. In Nigeria, NAFDAC regulates herbal products; other countries have their own regulators. Check national guidance.

keyPoints: Pharmacognosy studies medicines from natural sources, especially plants.
A crude drug is natural material used as medicine with little processing.
Active constituents are the compounds mainly responsible for a plant’s effect; marker compounds help compare batches.
Standardisation checks identity, purity, strength and contamination to make batches consistent.
Herbal medicines can cause harm and interact with medicines; natural does not mean safe.
Traditional medicine is regulated nationally; check current national guidance and WHO advice.

en.title: Principles of pharmacology
en.short: Receptors, agonists and antagonists, dose-response, ADME, variability, interactions and adverse effects.

sections.heading: Receptors and ligands
sections.text: A receptor is a protein that binds a ligand and starts a response. Affinity is binding strength. Efficacy is the ability to produce a response. A full agonist has high efficacy, a partial agonist lower efficacy, and an inverse agonist reduces constitutive activity (receptor activity with no ligand bound). An antagonist binds with affinity but has no efficacy. Competitive antagonists shift the dose-response curve right and can be overcome by more agonist. Noncompetitive antagonists reduce the maximum response. Spare receptors can allow maximum response before full occupancy.

sections.heading: Dose and response
sections.text: A graded dose-response curve plots response against dose or concentration. On a log scale it is sigmoid. EC50 is the concentration producing half the maximum response, and Emax is the maximum. Potency describes position, so a lower EC50 means greater potency. Efficacy describes height. A quantal curve plots the proportion of subjects responding. Therapeutic index compares toxic with effective exposure; a narrow index means less separation and more monitoring.

sections.heading: Pharmacokinetics
sections.text: Pharmacokinetics describes absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion. Absorption moves drug into blood. Distribution moves it to tissues. Metabolism, mainly hepatic, usually inactivates drug but can activate prodrugs or form active metabolites; excretion, mainly renal and biliary, removes it. Bioavailability is the fraction reaching systemic circulation. Volume of distribution is a theoretical volume. Clearance is the volume cleared per unit time. Half-life is the time for concentration to halve. After n half-lives, fraction remaining is (1/2)^n. Example: with a 6-hour half-life, after 24 hours n = 24 ÷ 6 = 4, so fraction remaining = (1/2)^4 = 1/16 = 0.0625, or 6.25%.

sections.heading: Variability and safety
sections.text: Response varies with age, weight, genetics, organ function, pregnancy, food, adherence and disease. Interactions are pharmacokinetic when they change absorption, distribution, metabolism or excretion, and pharmacodynamic when they add or oppose effects. Adverse effects may be predictable and dose-related or unpredictable, such as immune and idiosyncratic reactions. Report suspected reactions to the national regulator. Guidelines differ by country and change, so check current national or WHO guidance. This summary teaches principles only, not medical advice or dosing.

keyPoints: Affinity is binding strength; efficacy is the ability to produce a response.
Competitive antagonists shift the dose-response curve right; noncompetitive antagonists reduce the maximum response.
EC50 measures potency; Emax measures efficacy.
ADME determines drug concentration over time; bioavailability, clearance, volume of distribution and half-life summarise it.
After n half-lives, fraction remaining = (1/2)^n; a 6-hour half-life leaves 6.25% after 24 hours.
Variability and interactions change response; report adverse effects and check current national or WHO guidance.

en.title: Medicinal chemistry and drug design
en.short: Drug targets, structure-activity relationships, prodrugs, metabolism and lead optimisation.

sections.heading: Drug targets
sections.text: Most drugs act on four main target types: receptors, enzymes, ion channels and transporters. Some act on nucleic acids. A target is a molecule in the body whose activity a drug changes. Receptors receive chemical signals; enzymes catalyse reactions; ion channels control ion flow; transporters move molecules across membranes. Good targets are relevant to the disease and can be modulated safely. Selectivity matters: a drug should affect the intended target more than related targets, or unwanted effects appear.

sections.heading: Structure and activity
sections.text: Structure-activity relationship (SAR) is the study of how chemical structure changes biological activity. Medicinal chemists modify functional groups and measure the effect on potency, selectivity, solubility, metabolism and toxicity. Acidic and basic groups ionise at body pH and affect absorption. Hydrogen-bonding groups affect target binding. Lipophilic groups can improve membrane passage but may reduce solubility. Steric bulk can block or fit a binding pocket. A small change can alter several properties at once, so SAR is a balance.

sections.heading: Prodrugs and metabolism
sections.text: A prodrug is an inactive or less active derivative that is converted in the body to the active drug. This can improve absorption or reduce irritation. Enalapril is an ester prodrug hydrolysed to enalaprilat. Drug metabolism mainly occurs in the liver. Phase I reactions, often by cytochrome P450 enzymes, oxidise, reduce or hydrolyse drugs. Phase II reactions conjugate drugs with groups such as glucuronic acid, sulphate or acetyl, usually making them more water-soluble for excretion. Metabolism can inactivate a drug, activate a prodrug, or form toxic products. Genetic differences and interactions can change these pathways.

sections.heading: Lead optimisation and design
sections.text: Lead optimisation turns a weak hit into a candidate by improving potency, selectivity, pharmacokinetics and safety. Rational drug design uses target structure or known ligands. Structure-based design uses protein structures and docking; ligand-based design compares known active molecules and quantitative SAR. A lead with IC50 (half-maximal inhibitory concentration) 10 µM improved to 1 µM by adding a hydroxyl group is tenfold more potent, but solubility and selectivity need checking.

keyPoints: Drugs usually act on receptors, enzymes, ion channels or transporters.
SAR links chemical structure to potency, selectivity, solubility, metabolism and toxicity.
Functional groups affect ionisation, binding, lipophilicity and steric fit.
Prodrugs are converted in the body to active drugs; enalapril is an ester prodrug of enalaprilat.
Phase I metabolism often uses cytochrome P450; phase II conjugation increases water solubility.
Lead optimisation balances potency, selectivity, pharmacokinetics and safety, using structure-based or ligand-based design.

en.title: Biopharmaceutics and pharmacokinetics
en.short: ADME, bioavailability, bioequivalence, compartment models, half-life, clearance and TDM principles.

sections.heading: Absorption and bioavailability
sections.text: Biopharmaceutics studies how a dosage form releases drug and how the body absorbs it. Absorption is movement from the administration site into blood. It depends on solubility, permeability and formulation. First-pass metabolism (loss before reaching systemic blood) lowers bioavailability. Bioavailability (F) is the fraction of an extravascular dose reaching systemic circulation unchanged. For the same drug, F = (AUC oral × dose IV) ÷ (AUC IV × dose oral), where AUC is area under the concentration-time curve. Bioequivalence means two products have comparable rate and extent of absorption; regulatory limits vary.

sections.heading: Distribution and clearance
sections.text: Distribution is movement of drug from blood into tissues; volume of distribution (Vd) relates amount in the body to plasma concentration: Vd = amount ÷ concentration. Metabolism changes drug chemically, often to inactive or more water-soluble products. Excretion removes drug and metabolites. Clearance (Cl) is the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time. For a constant intravenous infusion at steady state, Cl = infusion rate ÷ steady-state concentration (Css).

sections.heading: Models and half-life
sections.text: Compartment models describe the body as one or more spaces. In a one-compartment model, drug distributes rapidly and plasma concentration falls exponentially. Half-life (t1/2) is the time for concentration to halve. For first-order elimination (rate proportional to concentration), t1/2 = 0.693 × Vd ÷ Cl. Example: if Vd is 40 L and Cl is 4 L/h, t1/2 = 0.693 × 40 ÷ 4 = 6.93 h. With a constant infusion of 20 mg/h, Css = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 mg/L.

sections.heading: Therapeutic monitoring
sections.text: Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) measures drug concentrations to guide therapy for drugs with a narrow therapeutic range, marked pharmacokinetic variability or a clear concentration-effect relationship. Principles: sample at the correct time, usually at steady state; record the dose and sampling time; interpret with clinical state, adherence, organ function and interacting drugs; and act within local protocols. TDM supports, not replaces, clinical judgement; target ranges differ between laboratories and countries.

keyPoints: Bioavailability is the fraction of an extravascular dose reaching systemic circulation unchanged; for the same drug, F = (AUC oral × dose IV) ÷ (AUC IV × dose oral).
Bioequivalence compares the rate and extent of absorption of two products, usually using AUC and peak concentration, within the limits set by the relevant regulator.
Volume of distribution relates the amount of drug in the body to plasma concentration: Vd = amount ÷ concentration.
Clearance is the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time; at steady state during constant intravenous infusion, Cl = infusion rate ÷ Css.
For first-order elimination, half-life is t1/2 = 0.693 × Vd ÷ Cl.
Therapeutic drug monitoring requires correct sampling time, usually at steady state, and interpretation with the patient’s clinical state and local target ranges.

en.title: Pharmaceutical formulation and manufacturing
en.short: It covers preformulation, excipients, tablets, capsules, liquids, sterile products, stability, scale-up, GMP and QbD.

sections.heading: Preformulation and excipients
sections.text: Preformulation studies the drug substance before formulation: solubility, polymorphism (different crystal forms), particle size, flow, compressibility and stability. These guide the dosage form and excipients, the non-active ingredients. Excipient roles include diluents (bulk), binders (hold granules), disintegrants (break tablets), lubricants and glidants (aid processing), preservatives, antioxidants, buffers and tonicity agents. Excipients must suit the drug, route, patient group and cost.

sections.heading: Tablets, capsules and liquids
sections.text: Tablets are commonly made by granulation and compression, or by direct compression, and are often coated. Tests include weight uniformity, hardness, friability, disintegration and dissolution. Hard capsules are filled with powder, granules or pellets; soft capsules may hold liquids. Liquid forms include solutions, suspensions and emulsions, and need pH control, viscosity, preservation and light protection. Worked example: if a blend is 20% w/w drug and each tablet weighs 250 mg, drug per tablet = 0.20 × 250 mg = 50 mg.

sections.heading: Sterile products and stability
sections.text: Sterile products include injections, eye drops and irrigation fluids. They are made by terminal sterilisation where possible, or by aseptic processing in cleanrooms. Control covers microbial contamination, pyrogens (fever-causing substances), particles, containers and water for injection. Stability testing studies how temperature, humidity and light affect quality over time. It sets shelf life and storage conditions. ICH stability guidance is applied through national regulators, and requirements differ by country and product.

sections.heading: Scale-up, GMP and QbD
sections.text: Scale-up moves a formula from laboratory to pilot and production scale. Mixing, granulation and compression must stay within defined ranges. Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) is the quality system that ensures products are made consistently to specification. It covers premises, equipment, documentation, validation, staff training and quality control. WHO publishes GMP guidance, and national regulators enforce their own rules, such as NAFDAC in Nigeria and the MHRA in the UK. Quality by design (QbD) starts with a quality target product profile, identifies critical quality attributes and critical process parameters, and uses risk assessment and design space to build quality into the process.

keyPoints: Preformulation matches drug properties to the dosage form and excipients.
Excipients are non-active ingredients chosen for function, compatibility and route.
Tablet quality depends on granulation, compression and tests such as dissolution and friability.
Drug per tablet = fraction of drug in blend × tablet weight.
Sterile products need terminal sterilisation or aseptic processing plus pyrogen and particle control.
Stability testing sets shelf life; GMP and QbD build consistent quality into the process.

en.title: Pharmaceutical analysis and quality control
en.short: Pharmacopoeial methods, assay, dissolution, uniformity, validation, stability, impurities, QC and QA.

sections.heading: Pharmacopoeial methods
sections.text: A pharmacopoeia is an official collection of standards and analytical methods. Examples are the United States Pharmacopeia (USP), British Pharmacopoeia (BP), European Pharmacopoeia (Ph. Eur.) and WHO International Pharmacopoeia. A country may adopt one or publish its own. A monograph gives identity, assay, impurity limits and other tests. Official status and methods differ between countries and editions, so use the current text required by your regulator.

sections.heading: Assay and uniformity
sections.text:
Assay measures the active ingredient quantitatively, usually against a reference standard. Dissolution measures release from a solid oral dosage form into a specified medium under controlled conditions. Content uniformity checks individual units; it detects mixing or filling problems that an average assay can hide.

Worked assay example. A tablet is labelled 200 mg. The extract is made to 200.0 mL; 5.0 mL is diluted to 100.0 mL. A 50.0 micrograms/mL standard gives absorbance 0.500; the sample gives 0.490. Sample concentration = (0.490 ÷ 0.500) × 50.0 = 49.0 micrograms/mL. The 100.0 mL holds 49.0 × 100 = 4900 micrograms = 4.90 mg. This came from 5.0 mL, so the 200.0 mL holds 4.90 × (200.0 ÷ 5.0) = 196 mg. Label claim = (196 ÷ 200) × 100 = 98.0 percent.

sections.heading: Validation and stability
sections.text: Method validation shows a method is suitable for its purpose. Typical parameters are specificity, linearity and range, accuracy, precision, detection and quantitation limits, and robustness. Acceptance criteria must be set before validation. Stability testing stores samples under defined temperature, humidity and light conditions to establish shelf life and storage. It includes long-term and accelerated studies and tests degradation. Impurity limits are maximum allowed amounts of degradation products, residual solvents or elemental impurities. They come from monographs and regulator guidance, such as ICH impurity guidelines. Check current national and WHO requirements.

sections.heading: Quality control and assurance
sections.text: Quality control (QC) tests samples against specifications. Quality assurance (QA) is the wider system of documentation, validation, training, audits and corrective actions. QC tests the product; QA builds the system around it.

keyPoints: Pharmacopoeial monographs set official identity, assay, impurity and other tests; editions and legal status vary by country.
Assay measures active ingredient against a reference standard; percentage of label claim = (measured content ÷ label claim) × 100.
Dissolution measures release from a solid oral dosage form; content uniformity checks individual units.
Method validation covers specificity, linearity and range, accuracy, precision, detection and quantitation limits, and robustness.
Stability testing establishes shelf life and storage conditions under defined temperature, humidity and light.
QC tests samples against specifications; QA is the wider system of documentation, validation, training, audits and corrective actions.

en.title: Pharmaceutical microbiology and sterility assurance
en.short: This summary covers contamination, preservatives, sterilisation, aseptic processing, cleanrooms, assays and endotoxins.

sections.heading: Contamination and preservatives
sections.text: Microbial contamination is the presence of unwanted microorganisms in a product, material or environment. Sources include water, air, equipment, containers, people and biofilms in pipes. Contamination can spoil a product or cause infection. Multi-dose liquid products often contain antimicrobial preservatives, substances that limit microbial growth. Preservatives are not sterilants. Their activity must be shown in the final formulation, because pH, oil and water partition and the container can reduce it. A preservative efficacy test challenges the product with specified organisms. Follow current pharmacopoeial and national guidance.

sections.heading: Sterilisation and asepsis
sections.text: Sterilisation kills or removes all microorganisms. Moist heat in an autoclave suits aqueous products; dry heat suits glass and metal; radiation suits devices; filtration removes organisms from heat-labile liquids; ethylene oxide sterilises heat-sensitive items. Disinfection reduces but does not sterilise. The D-value is the time to reduce a population by one log, or 90 per cent. For example, a fall from 1,000,000 to 100 organisms is four logs; if this takes 20 minutes, the D-value is 5 minutes. Sterility assurance level (SAL) is the probability of a surviving organism; 10^-6 means one in a million. Aseptic processing assembles sterile components in a controlled way when terminal sterilisation would damage the product.

sections.heading: Cleanrooms, assays and endotoxins
sections.text: Cleanrooms control particles and microbial counts. High-efficiency particulate air (HEPA) filters clean the air. Grading schemes differ between regions, so check local good manufacturing practice (GMP). People are a major contamination source, so gowning and training matter. Environmental monitoring samples air, surfaces and personnel. Microbiological assays include sterility tests, microbial limit tests, antibiotic potency assays and preservative efficacy tests; they need method suitability checks. A sterility test examines only samples, so sterility is assured by process validation. Endotoxins are lipopolysaccharides from Gram-negative bacteria and are fever-causing pyrogens. They survive many sterilisation cycles, so equipment may need depyrogenation, often by dry heat. Bacterial endotoxin testing, such as the Limulus amoebocyte lysate (LAL) test, is used where pharmacopoeial limits apply. Check national and WHO guidance.

keyPoints: Microbial contamination comes from water, air, people, equipment and biofilms; preservatives only limit growth and must be efficacy-tested.
Sterilisation kills or removes all microorganisms; disinfection does not.
D-value is the time for a one-log (90 per cent) reduction; SAL 10^-6 means a one-in-a-million chance of a surviving organism.
Aseptic processing and cleanrooms rely on HEPA-filtered air, gowning, environmental monitoring and process validation.
Sterility tests examine samples only, so sterility assurance comes from validated processes.
Endotoxins are Gram-negative lipopolysaccharides and pyrogens; they need depyrogenation and are measured by tests such as LAL under pharmacopoeial limits.

en.title: Compounding and dispensing
en.short: Extemporaneous preparation, prescription reading, labelling, packaging, calculations, records and error prevention.

sections.heading: Prescription interpretation
sections.text: Dispensing is the process of supplying a medicine to a named patient after interpreting a prescription, preparing it if needed, labelling, packaging and recording. Read the whole prescription: patient identifiers, medicine, strength, quantity, directions, date and prescriber. If anything is unclear, incomplete or inconsistent, stop and clarify with the prescriber; never guess. Check for known allergies and for ingredients that may not suit the patient. Legal requirements for what a prescription must contain differ by country.

sections.heading: Extemporaneous preparation
sections.text:
Extemporaneous preparation is small-scale compounding for a named patient when no suitable commercial product exists or an authorised product cannot meet the need. Work from a written formula or pharmacopoeial method. Use a clean, organised area, calibrated balances and measures, and ingredients of known quality. Record the source and lot number of each ingredient. Consider stability, compatibility, preservative need and container.

Example: to make 120 g of a 2% w/w ointment from a 10% w/w stock and base, let x be stock mass. 0.10x = 0.02 × 120 = 2.4 g, so x = 24 g. Base = 120 − 24 = 96 g. Check: 2.4/120 = 0.02, or 2%.

sections.heading: Labelling and packaging
sections.text: Label the container before or immediately after preparation. Include patient name, product and strength, quantity, directions, date prepared, expiry or beyond-use date (the date after which a compounded product should not be used), storage advice, batch or preparation number and the pharmacy. Add cautionary labels where local rules require. Choose a container that protects the product from light, moisture or contamination and is safe for the patient. Child-resistant closures may be required. Keep the label legible and avoid abbreviations that could be misread.

sections.heading: Documentation and errors
sections.text: Document the formula, calculations, ingredients and lot numbers, quantities weighed or measured, yield, label copy, preparer, checker and any deviation. Keep records for the period required by the national regulator. Prevent errors with standard procedures, an independent check of calculations and final product, a quiet workspace, and read-back when clarifying prescriptions. Label one product at a time and never leave an unlabelled container. Report errors and near misses through the local system. Requirements vary, so follow current national guidance.

keyPoints: Dispensing means interpreting a prescription, preparing if needed, labelling, packaging and recording.
Extemporaneous preparation is small-scale compounding for a named patient when no suitable commercial product exists.
Clarify any unclear prescription instead of guessing.
For dilution, mass of stock = (final mass × final percentage) ÷ stock percentage.
Label immediately with patient, product, strength, directions, date, expiry and batch.
Document calculations and use independent checks to prevent errors; follow current national rules.

en.title: Pharmacy law, ethics and regulation
en.short: Medicines law, licensing, controlled drugs, consent, confidentiality and conflicts of interest.

sections.heading: Law and regulators
sections.text: Medicines law is national. It controls approval, manufacture, import, distribution, sale, advertising and safety reporting. A regulator enforces it. In Nigeria, NAFDAC regulates medicine products, while the Pharmacists Council of Nigeria regulates pharmacy practice and premises. In the United Kingdom, the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) regulates medicines and devices, while in Great Britain the General Pharmaceutical Council regulates pharmacy professionals and pharmacies. In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulates products, while state boards of pharmacy license practitioners and pharmacies. These bodies and their powers differ, so always check the current national law and official guidance. WHO guidance supports countries but does not replace national law.

sections.heading: Licensing and controlled medicines
sections.text: Licensing has several layers: a product needs a marketing authorisation (official approval to sell it) before sale; a pharmacy or wholesale dealer needs a premises licence; a pharmacist needs registration. Supplying outside these rules is illegal. Controlled medicines are drugs with extra legal controls because of abuse or dependence risk. Countries place them in schedules with different rules for prescribing, storage, record keeping and disposal. A schedule in one country does not apply in another. Pharmacists must follow the national controlled medicines law and keep accurate records that may be inspected.

sections.heading: Ethics and consent
sections.text: Professional ethics require competence, honesty and patient-centred judgement. Confidentiality means not disclosing patient information without consent or a legal exception. Consent must be voluntary, informed and given by someone with capacity; rules for children and adults lacking capacity vary by country. Conflicts of interest, such as gifts or personal payments from suppliers, must be declared and managed. For example, a pharmacist offered a personal bonus to recommend a supplier’s brand should decline and record the offer, because the patient’s interest comes first. National council codes and the FIP (International Pharmaceutical Federation) code give more detail.

keyPoints: Medicines law is national, and regulators and their powers differ by country.
Product authorisation, premises licensing and professional registration are separate requirements.
Controlled medicines have extra rules for prescribing, storage, records and disposal, and schedules differ by country.
Confidentiality can be broken only with consent or a legal exception.
Valid consent is voluntary, informed and given by a person with capacity.
Declare and manage conflicts of interest; the patient’s interest comes first.

en.title: Clinical pharmacy and patient care
en.short: Medication history, pharmaceutical care, review, counselling, adherence and referral.

sections.heading: Medication history
sections.text: Clinical pharmacy is patient-centred practice that seeks the best outcomes from medicines. A medication history is a structured account of every medicine a person uses: prescribed, bought, traditional, herbal and supplements. Record name, strength, dose, route, timing, reason, allergies and past reactions. Ask open questions, see actual medicines and containers, and check records and carers. Reconcile at admission, transfer and discharge: check the list matches what the person actually takes and what is prescribed. A good history prevents omissions and double dosing.

sections.heading: Pharmaceutical care
sections.text: Pharmaceutical care is the responsible provision of medicine therapy to achieve definite outcomes that improve quality of life. The pharmacist works with the patient and team, identifies medicine problems, sets goals and monitors results in a care plan. Medication review is a structured, critical examination of a person’s medicines with them. It checks whether each medicine has a valid indication, is effective, is safe and is taken. Use current national or WHO guidance, not memorised protocols.

sections.heading: Counselling and adherence
sections.text: Patient counselling explains the purpose of treatment, how to use it, common side effects, what to do about them, storage and follow-up. Use plain language and teach-back: ask the person to repeat the plan. Adherence is the extent to which a person takes medicines as agreed. Barriers may be unintentional (cost, complexity, forgetfulness) or intentional (beliefs, side effects). Ask without blame. Shared decision-making means explaining options and uncertainties, exploring the person’s values, and agreeing a plan together. It supports adherence but does not guarantee it.

sections.heading: Records and referral
sections.text: Documentation records the history, review findings, agreed plan, counselling, adherence and referrals. Write clearly, date and sign entries, and record in the patient’s record promptly. Refer when a problem is beyond your scope or a red flag (a warning sign of a possibly serious problem) appears: contact the prescriber or specialist, state the reason and urgency, and follow up. Case: Mrs Okafor brings several medicines. The pharmacist lists them, reviews them, counsels her, refers a worrying symptom and documents each step.

keyPoints: A medication history lists all prescribed, bought, traditional and herbal medicines, with allergies and past reactions.
Pharmaceutical care uses a documented care plan to identify medicine problems, set goals and monitor outcomes.
Medication review checks indication, effectiveness, safety and adherence against current national or WHO guidance.
Counselling should use plain language and teach-back, and adherence should be explored without blame.
Shared decision-making explains options and uncertainties and agrees a plan with the patient.
Document clearly and promptly, and refer promptly when a problem is beyond your scope or a red flag appears.

en.title: Pharmacotherapy of infectious diseases
en.short: Antimicrobial selection, stewardship, resistance, and management principles for malaria, HIV and TB.

sections.heading: Choosing antimicrobials
sections.text: An antimicrobial is a medicine that kills or stops microbes. Antibiotics act on bacteria, antivirals on viruses and antimalarials on malaria parasites. Selection starts with the likely cause, using history, examination and tests such as microscopy, culture or rapid tests. Empiric therapy begins before the cause is confirmed; targeted therapy is adjusted when results arrive. Choose the narrowest agent likely to work, considering infection site, local resistance data, allergies, kidney and liver function, pregnancy, interactions and cost. This is education, not medical advice.

sections.heading: Stewardship and resistance
sections.text: Antimicrobial stewardship is the coordinated effort to use antimicrobials only when needed, at the right dose, route and duration. It reduces resistance, which occurs when microbes survive treatment and multiply. Resistance is driven by unnecessary use, incomplete courses, poor quality medicines and spread of resistant strains. Stewardship includes guidelines, prescriber feedback, infection control and patient counselling. Example: in a hospital in Ibadan, Nigeria, a patient with a cold asks for antibiotics. The pharmacist explains that colds are viral, checks for red flags and advises rest and fluids. No antibiotic is supplied. Follow national and WHO guidance.

sections.heading: Malaria and HIV
sections.text: Malaria: confirm with a parasitological test before treatment. Treat according to species, severity and national policy. Uncomplicated falciparum malaria is usually treated with artemisinin-based combination therapy; severe malaria needs urgent parenteral therapy, often artesunate, and referral. HIV: antiretroviral therapy (ART) suppresses viral load, preserves immunity and prevents transmission. Adherence, viral load monitoring, resistance testing and screening for opportunistic infections are central. Pharmacists check interactions and counsel on adherence. Use current WHO or national guidelines.

sections.heading: Tuberculosis
sections.text: Tuberculosis (TB) needs a combination of medicines for a long period to prevent resistance. Treatment follows national TB programme and WHO guidance, with drug susceptibility testing where possible. Directly observed treatment or other treatment support helps adherence. Monitor for adverse effects and interactions with HIV medicines. Multidrug-resistant TB requires specialist regimens. Never use a single drug for active TB. Current guidance changes, so check the national programme.

keyPoints: Select antimicrobials using the likely cause, tests, local resistance data and patient factors; start empiric therapy only when justified.
Antimicrobial stewardship means using the right agent, dose, route and duration only when needed, supported by guidelines and infection control.
Resistance is driven by unnecessary use, poor adherence, poor quality medicines and cross-infection.

Confirm malaria before treatment when possible; use artemisinin-based combination therapy for uncomplicated falciparum malaria and urgent parenteral therapy for severe disease, following national or WHO guidance.
HIV care centres on adherence to antiretroviral therapy, viral load monitoring, resistance testing and screening for opportunistic infections.
Active tuberculosis needs a combination regimen for a long period, susceptibility testing and treatment support; never use a single drug.

en.title: Pharmacotherapy of non-communicable diseases
en.short: Principles of drug selection and monitoring in cardiovascular, respiratory, diabetes, mental health and pain.

sections.heading: Selection principles
sections.text:
Pharmacotherapy means using medicines to treat disease. Selection starts with a confirmed diagnosis and a clear goal, such as lowering blood pressure or preventing asthma attacks. Assess age, pregnancy, kidney and liver function, other diseases, interactions, adherence and cost.

Guidelines differ by country and change, so use current national or World Health Organization guidance and individualise. Monitoring is part of selection: decide what will show benefit or harm, such as symptoms, blood pressure, glucose or renal function.

sections.heading: Cardiovascular and respiratory
sections.text:
In cardiovascular disease, choose drugs for compelling indications. For example, an ACE inhibitor or ARB is often used in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction and diabetic kidney disease, and a beta blocker after myocardial infarction. Monitor blood pressure and lipids; check renal function and potassium with ACE inhibitors, ARBs and diuretics; monitor bleeding with anticoagulants.

In asthma, an inhaled corticosteroid is the cornerstone controller, and relievers treat symptoms. Review adherence, inhaler technique and exacerbations. In COPD, bronchodilators, smoking cessation and vaccination are central; monitor exacerbations and inhaler technique.

sections.heading: Diabetes and mental health
sections.text:
In type 2 diabetes, set an individualised glycaemic target. Metformin is often first-line unless contraindicated. SGLT2 inhibitors or GLP-1 receptor agonists may be chosen for cardiovascular or kidney protection in selected patients. Monitor HbA1c, renal function, weight and hypoglycaemia.

In mental health, assess symptom severity, suicide risk, comorbidity and interactions. Antidepressants take weeks to work, so review early for worsening and suicidal thoughts. Antipsychotics require monitoring of weight, glucose, lipids and movement effects. The WHO Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP) offers guidance.

sections.heading: Pain and a case
sections.text:
For pain, assess cause and severity. NSAIDs need caution in renal, cardiovascular and gastrointestinal risk. Opioids are for moderate to severe pain when other measures are not enough, with review, constipation prevention and dependence monitoring. The WHO analgesic ladder is a framework for cancer pain.

Amina, 58, in Kano has hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Her clinician checks renal function and potassium before starting an ACE inhibitor, and rechecks as local guidance advises. Her HbA1c and blood pressure are reviewed, and she is asked about dizziness or swelling.

keyPoints: Confirm the diagnosis and assess comorbidity, kidney and liver function, interactions and adherence before choosing a medicine.
Guidelines differ by country and change, so use current national or WHO guidance and individualise.
In asthma, inhaled corticosteroids are the cornerstone controller; check inhaler technique and adherence.
In type 2 diabetes, individualise glycaemic targets and monitor renal function, hypoglycaemia and cardiovascular risk.
Antidepressants and antipsychotics need early review for worsening symptoms, suicide risk and metabolic effects.
For pain, assess cause and use multimodal treatment; review opioids and monitor NSAID risks.

en.title: Pharmacovigilance and drug safety
en.short: Adverse reactions, reporting, causality, signals, medication errors and risk management.

sections.heading: Reactions and errors
sections.text:
Pharmacovigilance is the science of detecting, assessing, understanding and preventing adverse effects or any other drug-related problem. An adverse drug reaction (ADR) is a harmful, unintended response to a medicine at normal doses. Type A reactions are predictable and dose-related, such as bleeding with an anticoagulant. Type B reactions are unpredictable and not clearly dose-related, such as an unusual allergic reaction.

A medication error is a preventable mistake in prescribing, dispensing, giving or monitoring a medicine. It may cause harm or none. An error is not the same as an ADR, though an error can lead to one.

sections.heading: Reporting and causality
sections.text:
Reports go to the national regulator, which forwards them to the WHO programme managed by the Uppsala Monitoring Centre, whose database is VigiBase. Health workers, patients and companies can all report. Underreporting is the main weakness, so reports are wanted even when causation is uncertain.

Causality assessment judges how likely the medicine caused the event. The WHO-UMC scale uses the categories certain, probable, possible, unlikely, conditional and unassessable. It weighs timing, whether the event is a known reaction, and what happens when the medicine is stopped (dechallenge) or given again (rechallenge).

sections.heading: Signals and risk management
sections.text: A signal is new information suggesting a possible causal link between a medicine and an event, not yet confirmed. Detection compares reported events with what would be expected; more reports than expected prompt review. Risk management uses measures such as label changes, training or restricted prescribing, reviewed as evidence grows.

sections.heading: African settings
sections.text: Many African countries run national centres, for example NAFDAC in Nigeria and SAHPRA in South Africa. Common challenges are few reporters, limited laboratory capacity and large informal medicine markets. Falsified and substandard medicines are a related safety concern and should be reported to the regulator.

keyPoints: Pharmacovigilance covers detection, assessment and prevention of drug-related harm.
Type A reactions are predictable and dose-related; Type B are unpredictable.
A medication error is preventable and is not the same as an ADR.
The WHO-UMC scale grades causality from certain to unassessable.
A signal is a possible link not yet confirmed.
Underreporting is the main weakness of reporting systems.

en.title: Community and hospital pharmacy practice
en.short: Roles and workflow in community and hospital pharmacy, from prescriptions to sterile services and safety.

sections.heading: Community pharmacy
sections.text: Community pharmacy is often a person’s first contact with the health system. The pharmacist dispenses prescriptions, gives advice on safe use, sells over-the-counter medicines, triages minor problems and refers when needed. Workflow usually runs from receiving and validating the prescription, checking legal and clinical details, preparing and labelling, a final check, counselling, and recording. Stock must be stored correctly, with expiry dates and cold-chain items monitored. Rules on prescribing, sales and records differ by country, so check national pharmacy law and regulator guidance.

sections.heading: Hospital workflow
sections.text: Hospital pharmacy serves inpatients and outpatients. Prescriptions are screened for allergies, interactions and suitability before dispensing. The hospital formulary is the approved list of medicines chosen by a committee for safety, effectiveness and cost; a non-formulary medicine needs approval. Inventory control uses reorder levels, stock rotation, expiry checks and audits to avoid shortages and waste. Ward pharmacy brings the pharmacist to the ward to review medication charts, reconcile medicines at admission and discharge, and answer questions from doctors and nurses.

sections.heading: Sterile services and safety
sections.text: Sterile services prepare products that must be free from microbes, such as intravenous additives, parenteral nutrition and cytotoxic medicines. This work needs cleanrooms, validated aseptic technique, environmental monitoring, trained staff and independent checks. Patient safety depends on reporting errors and near misses, using at least two patient identifiers, checking labels and expiry dates, and managing look-alike and sound-alike names. Case: Amina is admitted after a fall. The ward pharmacist compares her home medicines with the admission chart and finds one omitted. She discusses it with the prescriber and records the discrepancy.

sections.heading: Working together
sections.text: Interprofessional working means doctors, nurses, pharmacists and supply staff share clear records and hand over safely. Pharmacists clarify unclear prescriptions and explain formulary choices. A no-blame reporting culture helps the system learn. National rules and WHO guidance on medication safety change, so always check current official guidance.

keyPoints: Community pharmacy workflow runs from prescription validation through dispensing, checking, counselling and recording.
Hospital formularies list approved medicines and guide safe, cost-effective prescribing.
Inventory control uses reorder levels, stock rotation, expiry checks and audits.
Ward pharmacists review charts and reconcile medicines at admission and discharge.
Sterile services need cleanrooms, validated aseptic technique and independent checks.
Patient safety and interprofessional working depend on clear records, error reporting and checking current national guidance.

en.title: Drug supply management and public health pharmacy
en.short: Procurement, storage, stock control, cold chain, essential medicines, rational use and immunisation roles.

sections.heading: Procurement and access
sections.text: Procurement is choosing, buying and receiving medicines. Good procurement is transparent, competitive and based on quantified need: estimate use from past consumption and expected cases. Buy from suppliers approved by the national regulator, and check quality, expiry and documents. An essential medicines list names products meeting priority health needs, chosen for efficacy, safety and cost-effectiveness. The World Health Organization (WHO) publishes a model list; each country adapts its own. Access means affordable, quality medicines are available when needed. It depends on price, supply, distance and prescribing. Check current national lists and guidance.

sections.heading: Storage and cold chain
sections.text: Storage protects quality. Keep stores dry, clean, secure and out of sunlight. Separate expired, damaged and recalled stock. Use first expiry, first out (FEFO): the earliest expiry leaves first. Record temperature regularly. The cold chain is the system of refrigerators, cold boxes and monitored transport that keeps heat-sensitive products, especially most vaccines, at the required temperature, commonly +2 to +8 °C; check the product label and national guidance. Plan for power cuts. Do not freeze vaccines unless the label allows it.

sections.heading: Stock control
sections.text: Stock control keeps records and quantities accurate. Use bin cards or stock cards and regular physical counts. Track expiry dates and slow-moving items. Set a reorder level so you order before stock runs out. Formula: reorder level = (average daily consumption × lead time in days) + safety stock. Example: a clinic uses 40 packs a day, waits 14 days for delivery, and keeps 120 packs as safety stock (buffer stock). Reorder level = (40 × 14) + 120 = 560 + 120 = 680 packs. When stock reaches 680 packs, order. Check against local policy.

sections.heading: Rational use and public health
sections.text: Rational medicine use means the right medicine, dose, route and duration for the patient, supported by guidelines, counselling and antimicrobial stewardship, the careful use of antibiotics. Health promotion includes adherence support, lifestyle advice and vaccination information. Pharmacists may store, distribute and, where national law allows, administer vaccines; roles differ by country. Check current national immunisation and regulator guidance.

keyPoints: Procurement should be transparent, competitive and based on quantified need from approved suppliers.
An essential medicines list selects products for priority health needs using efficacy, safety and cost-effectiveness.
Use FEFO in stores and monitor cold chain temperature; most vaccines need +2 to +8 °C unless the label says otherwise.
Reorder level = (average daily consumption × lead time) + safety stock.
Rational medicine use means the right medicine, dose, route and duration, supported by counselling and stewardship.
Pharmacists’ immunisation roles vary by country; check national law and current immunisation guidance.

en.title: Research methods and biostatistics in pharmacy
en.short: Study designs, sampling, bias, statistics, critical appraisal, ethics and scientific writing.

sections.heading: Designs and sampling
sections.text:
Research methods turn a pharmacy question into a testable plan. Observational designs do not assign treatment: cross-sectional surveys measure exposure and outcome at one time; cohort studies follow groups forward; case-control studies compare people with an outcome to controls. Experimental designs assign an intervention; the randomised controlled trial is strongest for causal questions when feasible and ethical.

Sampling is how participants are chosen. Probability methods, such as simple random, stratified and cluster sampling, give eligible people a known chance of selection. Convenience sampling limits generalisation. Justify sample size in advance.

sections.heading: Bias and description
sections.text:
Bias is systematic error that pushes results away from the truth. Selection bias arises when the sample differs from the target population. Information bias arises from inaccurate measurement or recall. Confounding occurs when a third factor is linked to both exposure and outcome. Random error is chance variation and shrinks as sample size grows.

Descriptive statistics summarise data. For numerical data, report mean and standard deviation for symmetric data, or median and interquartile range for skewed data. For categorical data, report counts and percentages.

sections.heading: Inference and appraisal
sections.text:
