Inferential statistics estimate population values and test hypotheses. A 95% confidence interval gives a range that would contain the true value in about 95% of repeated samples. A p value is the probability of results at least as extreme as those observed if the null hypothesis were true; it is not the probability that the null is true. For example, if 40 of 100 treated patients improve and 25 of 100 controls improve, the ratio of the two risks is 0.40 ÷ 0.25 = 1.6.

Critical appraisal asks whether a study is valid and whether it applies to your patients.

sections.heading: Ethics and writing
sections.text: Research ethics requires informed consent, confidentiality, and approval from an ethics committee before data collection. Do not fabricate or plagiarise. Scientific writing usually follows IMRaD: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion. State the question, methods and limitations clearly so others can judge and repeat the work.

keyPoints: Observational studies describe or follow people; randomised trials assign treatment and can support causal claims.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; convenience sampling limits it.
Bias is systematic error; random error is chance variation.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; standard deviation summarises spread for symmetric numerical data.
Risk ratio = risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed; a 95% confidence interval estimates the population value, and a p value is not the probability that the null is true.
Critical appraisal checks validity and applicability; ethics approval, informed consent and honest reporting are required, and scientific writing follows IMRaD.

en.title: Advanced pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics
en.short: Covers nonlinear kinetics, PK/PD models, therapeutic drug monitoring and population approaches.

sections.heading: Nonlinear kinetics
sections.text:
Most drugs follow first-order kinetics: clearance is constant and half-life does not change with concentration. In nonlinear (capacity-limited) kinetics, a saturable enzyme or transporter limits elimination. The Michaelis-Menten rate is Vmax × C ÷ (Km + C). At low C the rate is first-order; at high C it approaches zero-order, so small dose increases can cause large concentration rises. Clearance and half-life then depend on concentration.

Ethanol and phenytoin are standard examples.

sections.heading: Modelling approaches
sections.text:
Compartmental models describe the body as one or more well-mixed compartments linked by rate constants. A one-compartment intravenous bolus gives C = C0 × e^(−kt). Noncompartmental analysis uses the concentration-time curve: AUC by the trapezoidal rule, terminal slope for k, and mean residence time from AUMC ÷ AUC.

Example: concentrations 10, 6 and 2 mg/L at 0, 2 and 4 h give AUC(0-4) = (10+6)÷2×2 + (6+2)÷2×2 = 24 mg·h/L. Terminal k = ln(6÷2)÷2 = 0.549 h−1, so half-life = ln2÷k ≈ 1.26 h.

sections.heading: PD and PK/PD
sections.text:
Pharmacodynamic models link concentration to effect. The Emax model is E = Emax × C ÷ (EC50 + C); the sigmoid Emax adds a Hill exponent. An effect compartment model allows for delay between plasma concentration and response. Indirect response models describe effects on production or loss of a mediator.

PK/PD indices include time above a threshold, peak÷threshold and AUC÷threshold. These guide dose regimen design, but target values differ by drug and pathogen and must come from current guidance.

sections.heading: TDM and population
sections.text:
Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) measures concentration to individualise therapy for drugs with narrow therapeutic ranges, poor predictability or concentration-dependent toxicity. Design requires the right sampling time, usually at steady state; trough samples are common, but timing depends on the drug and formulation.

Population pharmacokinetics uses data from many patients to estimate typical clearance and variability; Bayesian methods combine this prior with a patient’s samples to estimate individual parameters. National TDM guidance varies, so check the current official protocol.

keyPoints: First-order elimination has constant clearance; nonlinear elimination follows Vmax × C ÷ (Km + C), becoming zero-order at high concentration.
Compartmental models use rate constants; a one-compartment bolus gives C = C0 × e^(−kt).
Noncompartmental analysis estimates AUC by the trapezoidal rule and mean residence time as AUMC ÷ AUC.
Emax and sigmoid Emax models link concentration to effect; effect compartment models account for delay.
TDM sampling must be timed to steady state and the drug’s formulation, following current national guidance.
Population pharmacokinetics estimates typical parameters and variability; Bayesian methods individualise from sparse samples.

en.title: Pharmaceutical biotechnology and nanomedicine
en.short: Biologics, antibodies, vaccines, gene delivery, nanoparticles, liposomes, characterisation, stability and regulation.

sections.heading: Biologics and antibodies
sections.text: Biologics are medicines made by living cells, often large proteins produced by recombinant DNA technology. They include hormones, enzymes, cytokines and monoclonal antibodies. A monoclonal antibody is a single antibody clone that binds one specific epitope, the target site on an antigen. It may be mouse, chimeric, humanised or fully human. Biosimilars are follow-on biologics, not generic copies: they need comparability studies. Case: pharmacist Amina at a hospital in Kenya reviews a biosimilar monoclonal antibody for lymphoma; she checks national regulator approval and comparability data before use.

sections.heading: Vaccines and gene delivery
sections.text: Vaccines train the immune system using live attenuated, inactivated, subunit, viral vector or mRNA platforms. Cold chain is critical. Gene delivery introduces genetic material into cells to treat disease. Viral vectors, such as adeno-associated virus, are efficient but have safety limits. Non-viral methods include lipid nanoparticles and electroporation. Case: a Nigerian immunisation team uses a vaccine vial monitor and keeps vaccines at the recommended temperature; if a vial’s monitor reaches its discard point, they discard that vial under national guidance.

sections.heading: Nanoparticles and liposomes
sections.text: Nanoparticles are carriers between about 1 and 100 nm. They can improve solubility, protect drugs and target tissues. Liposomes are vesicles with a lipid bilayer; water-soluble drugs sit in the core and fat-soluble drugs in the bilayer. PEGylation, attaching polyethylene glycol, lengthens circulation. Example: 2 mg drug in 18 mg lipid gives a drug-to-lipid ratio of 1:9 and a loading of 2 ÷ 20 = 10% w/w. Liposomal amphotericin B is used for visceral leishmaniasis in East Africa, though the standard first-line there is usually a combination of other medicines.

sections.heading: Characterisation and regulation
sections.text: Characterisation measures size, size distribution, surface charge (zeta potential), drug loading, release and structure. Stability studies test aggregation, degradation and container interactions; many biologics need cold chain. Regulation covers quality, safety and efficacy. WHO and national agencies, such as NAFDAC in Nigeria and the EMA in Europe, provide guidance. Clinical protocols change, so check current national or WHO guidance. This is education, not medical advice.

keyPoints: Biologics are made in living cells; biosimilars are not generic copies and need comparability data.
Monoclonal antibodies bind one epitope and may be chimeric, humanised or fully human.
Vaccines use live attenuated, inactivated, subunit, viral vector or mRNA platforms and depend on the cold chain.
Gene delivery uses viral or non-viral vectors; targeting and safety are the main limits.
Liposomes carry water-soluble drugs in the core and fat-soluble drugs in the bilayer; drug loading = mass of drug ÷ total mass × 100%.
Characterisation, stability testing and national or WHO regulatory guidance are required before clinical use.

en.title: Advanced clinical pharmacy and pharmaceutical care
en.short: Complex patients, reconciliation, deprescribing, stewardship, safety leadership and guideline appraisal.

sections.heading: Complex patients
sections.text:
Advanced clinical pharmacy applies pharmaceutical care, a patient-centred practice in which the pharmacist takes responsibility for a person’s medicine-related needs, to complex patients. These include people with multimorbidity, polypharmacy, frailty, cognitive impairment, or kidney and liver disease. Their risk is higher because medicines interact and care moves between home, clinic and hospital.

Medication reconciliation is a structured comparison of the medicines a person takes with the new prescription at a transition of care. The pharmacist checks adherence and allergies, identifies omissions, duplicates and wrong doses, and resolves discrepancies. It needs a clear owner and a documented process.

sections.heading: Deprescribing and stewardship
sections.text: Deprescribing is the planned, supervised withdrawal of a medicine when its harms now outweigh its benefits, for example in frailty or advanced illness. It requires shared decision-making, tapering where needed, and monitoring for withdrawal effects or return of symptoms. Antimicrobial stewardship is a coordinated programme to improve antibiotic use: right indication, agent, dose, route and duration, with review and de-escalation. It reduces resistance and harm. Follow current national and WHO guidance, not memorised protocols.

sections.heading: Safety and guidelines
sections.text: Medication safety leadership means pharmacists lead system improvements, not only individual checks. A just culture encourages reporting of errors and near misses, then analyses causes. High-alert medicines, look-alike names and transitions of care need stronger defences. Guideline appraisal means judging whether a guideline is trustworthy and applicable: check the date, authors, evidence base, conflicts of interest and local feasibility. Tools such as GRADE and AGREE II help, but do not replace clinical judgement.

sections.heading: Interprofessional practice
sections.text: Interprofessional practice is team-based care in which pharmacists, doctors, nurses and others share goals and communicate clearly. A case: Mrs Okafor, 78, is admitted with confusion. She takes eight medicines. The pharmacist reconciles and finds an unintended duplicate and an omitted heart medicine. The team reviews each medicine, considers deprescribing one without a current indication, and stops an antibiotic lacking infection evidence after stewardship review. The plan is documented and shared with community pharmacy and family.

keyPoints: Pharmaceutical care makes the pharmacist responsible for a person’s medicine-related needs.
Medication reconciliation compares the medicines a person takes with new prescriptions at care transitions and resolves discrepancies.
Deprescribing is planned, supervised withdrawal when harms outweigh benefits, with monitoring.
Antimicrobial stewardship improves antibiotic use and reduces resistance; follow current national and WHO guidance.
Medication safety leadership uses a just culture and system defences, not blame.
Guideline appraisal checks quality, currency and applicability, and interprofessional practice shares goals and communication.

en.title: Advanced research methods and the pharmacy dissertation
en.short: Study design, protocol, ethics, data management, analysis, writing and dissemination for a pharmacy dissertation.

sections.heading: Design and protocol
sections.text:
At master’s level, justify the design. A randomised controlled trial tests an intervention by random allocation, which balances known and unknown confounders. A cohort follows exposed and unexposed people over time. A case-control compares people with and without an outcome, useful for rare outcomes. Cross-sectional studies measure exposure and outcome at one time. Qualitative interviews or focus groups explore meaning and experience. Mixed methods combine numbers and narratives.

A protocol is written before data collection. It states the question, design, population, sampling, variables, outcomes, analysis plan and limitations. Pre-specify the primary outcome to reduce selective reporting. Case: a student studies antihypertensive adherence in a teaching hospital using a survey and interviews. The protocol fixes the adherence measure, sampling frame and interview guide before ethics approval.

sections.heading: Ethics and data
sections.text:
Ethics approval is required before recruitment. An ethics committee, or institutional review board, checks consent, confidentiality, risk and benefit, and protection of vulnerable people. Requirements differ by country and institution, so check current national rules and WHO or CIOMS guidance. Obtain written informed consent unless a committee approves a waiver. Submit amendments before changing the protocol.

A data management plan names who owns the data, how it is collected, coded, stored, backed up and shared. Use unique identifiers, encryption and an audit trail. Anonymise personal data early. Keep records for the period required by your institution or funder. Missing data and data entry errors must be recorded, not hidden.

sections.heading: Analysis and writing
sections.text:
Statistical analysis follows the pre-specified plan. Describe baseline data, then estimate effect sizes with confidence intervals. For example, if 30 of 100 exposed and 15 of 100 unexposed have an outcome, the risk ratio is
(30/100) ÷ (15/100) = 2.0.
Report missing data and sensitivity analyses. Qualitative analysis uses coding and themes, with quotes as evidence.

Scientific writing follows IMRaD: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion. Use reporting guidelines such as CONSORT, STROBE or COREQ. Disseminate through the dissertation, a conference and a plain-language summary for participants.

keyPoints: Justify the design: trials test interventions, cohorts follow exposure, case-control suits rare outcomes, and qualitative work explores experience.
Write and pre-specify a protocol before data collection, including the primary outcome and analysis plan.
Obtain ethics approval before recruitment; requirements differ by country and institution.
Use a data management plan with unique identifiers, encryption, backup and an audit trail.
Analyse according to the plan; for a 2×2 table, risk ratio = (a/(a+b)) ÷ (c/(c+d)).
Write in IMRaD style, follow reporting guidelines, and disseminate to participants and the public.
